## Overview

The `wnpmle` package implements the **weighted nonparametric maximum likelihood
estimator (wNPMLE)** for the marginal mean of recurrent events in the presence
of a competing terminal event.

Competing events are commonly modeled as independent right-censorings, which
leads to overestimation of the marginal mean of a recurrent event. `wnpmle`
provides valid estimation and prediction via a weighted nonparametric maximum
likelihood estimation for two broad classes of semiparametric transformation
models.

| Models | Link function G(x) | Special cases |
|-------|---------------------|---------------|
| Box-Cox transformation models (`model = "boxcox"`) | $((1 + x)^\rho - 1)/\rho$ | Ghosh–Lin ($\rho = 1$); $\log(1+x)$ as $\rho \to 0$ |
| Logarithmic transformation models (`model = "log"`) | $\log(1 + r x)/r$ | Proportional odds ($r = 1$); Ghosh–Lin as $r \to 0$ |

Both are estimated via automatic differentiation using TMB, which provides
exact gradients and fast convergence. The compiled TMB code is cached, so it is
compiled only once after installation.

---

## Installation

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("wnpmle")
```

Or from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("abellach/wnpmle")
```

---

## Quick start: bladder tumour data

Ghosh and Lin (2002) illustrated their marginal model on the bladder tumour
trial of the Veterans Administration Cooperative Urological Research Group,
comparing thiotepa with placebo and adjusting for the number of tumours and
the size of the largest tumour at baseline. `bladder_prep()` prepares these
two arms of the `bladder1` data from the `survival` package. The Box-Cox
model with $\rho = 1$ is the Ghosh–Lin model.

```{r quick}
library(wnpmle)

bdata <- bladder_prep()
fit_bladder <- wnpmle_fit(
  Surv(time, status) ~ treat + num + size,
  data  = bdata,
  id    = "id",
  model = "boxcox",
  rho   = 1,
  tau   = 59
)
fit_bladder
```

The estimates are close to those reported by Ghosh and Lin (2002, Table 5,
IPCW estimator of the marginal mean):

```{r quick-compare}
data.frame(
  Ghosh_Lin_est = c(-0.560, 0.170, 0.003),
  Ghosh_Lin_se  = c(0.267, 0.060, 0.044),
  wnpmle_est    = round(coef(fit_bladder), 3),
  wnpmle_se     = round(fit_bladder$se, 3)
)
```

Small differences are expected: Ghosh and Lin solve estimating equations,
whereas `wnpmle` maximizes a weighted likelihood, and the data preparation
may differ slightly.

## Example: hospital readmissions after colorectal cancer surgery

The `readmission` data (Gonzalez et al., 2005) contain repeated hospital
readmissions of 403 patients after surgery for colorectal cancer. Death is a
competing terminal event: after death no further readmissions can occur. The
data are widely used for recurrent events with a terminal event, for example
in the joint frailty models of the `frailtypack` package. `readmission_prep()`
returns them in the format used by `wnpmle_fit()`: one row per readmission
(status 1) and one final row per patient, either death (status 2) or
censoring (status 0). Time is measured in days since surgery.

```{r readmission-data}
rdata <- readmission_prep(tau = 1460)
head(rdata)
table(rdata$status)
```

The covariates are chemotherapy, sex, Dukes' tumour stage and the Charlson
comorbidity index. The Charlson index is time-dependent: it may change
between readmissions, and each row carries the value recorded for that
interval.

Previous analyses of these data consider horizons of several years after
surgery. We end follow-up at $\tau = 4$ years (1460 days) with
`readmission_prep(tau = 1460)`: readmissions after $\tau$ are dropped and
patients still under observation are censored at $\tau$. At that time 25% of
the patients are still followed and 98% of the readmissions have occurred.
Beyond $\tau$ the number of patients at risk drops rapidly (21 patients at
5 years), and the nonparametric estimate of the baseline mean, which has a
jump at every readmission, becomes unstable.

### Choosing the transformation

`plot_loglik()` fits the model over a grid of transformation parameters and
plots the profile log-likelihood for both model classes. The logarithmic
parameter $r$ is shown on the left (mirrored axis), the Box-Cox parameter
$\rho$ on the right. The open circle marks the Ghosh–Lin model ($\rho = 1$),
the filled circle the proportional odds model ($r = 1$). Note that the two
curves do not have to meet at zero: $\rho \to 0$ corresponds to $r = 1$, and
$r \to 0$ corresponds to $\rho = 1$.

```{r loglik-plot, eval = FALSE}
plot_loglik(
  Surv(time, status) ~ chemo + sex + dukes + charlson,
  data     = rdata,
  id       = "id",
  tau      = 1460,
  rho_grid = seq(0.05, 1.2, by = 0.05),
  r_grid   = seq(0.05, 1.2, by = 0.05)
)
```

```{r loglik-figure, echo = FALSE, out.width = "85%", fig.align = "center"}
knitr::include_graphics("loglik_readmission.png")
```

The 48 fits take well under a minute. The maxima are at
$\hat\rho \approx 0.85$ in the Box-Cox class and $\hat r \approx 0.15$ in the
logarithmic class (log-likelihoods $-3016.69$ and $-3016.52$), both close to the
Ghosh–Lin model ($\rho = 1$, equivalently $r \to 0$), which fits practically
as well. The Box-Cox curve is flat between about 0.6 and 1.2, so the data do not
distinguish values in this range. The proportional odds model ($r = 1$) fits
clearly worse, about 5 log-likelihood units below the optimum. The exact optima can be found with
`optimize()`, for example

```{r optimize, eval = FALSE}
f <- function(p) wnpmle_fit(Surv(time, status) ~ chemo + sex + dukes + charlson,
                            data = rdata, id = "id", model = "boxcox", rho = p,
                            tau = 1460, se = "none")$loglik
optimize(f, interval = c(0.2, 1), maximum = TRUE)
```

### Fitting the selected model

```{r fit-readmission}
fit_rd <- wnpmle_fit(
  Surv(time, status) ~ chemo + sex + dukes + charlson,
  data  = rdata,
  id    = "id",
  model = "boxcox",
  rho   = 0.85,
  tau   = 1460,
  se    = "sandwich_adj"
)
summary(fit_rd)
```

For comparison, the Ghosh–Lin and proportional odds models:

```{r compare}
fit_gl <- wnpmle_fit(Surv(time, status) ~ chemo + sex + dukes + charlson,
                     data = rdata, id = "id", model = "boxcox", rho = 1,
                     tau = 1460, se = "none")
fit_po <- wnpmle_fit(Surv(time, status) ~ chemo + sex + dukes + charlson,
                     data = rdata, id = "id", model = "log", rho = 1,
                     tau = 1460, se = "none")
sapply(list(boxcox_0.85 = fit_rd, ghosh_lin = fit_gl, prop_odds = fit_po), AIC)
```

Chemotherapy, female sex and Dukes' stage D are clearly associated with the
expected number of readmissions. These effects refer to the **marginal mean**
number of readmissions, which accounts for the fact that patients who die
cannot be readmitted. Covariates that increase mortality therefore also lower
the marginal mean. In a joint frailty analysis of these data, chemotherapy was
associated with a markedly higher risk of death but not with the readmission
rate itself (Król et al., 2017), so the negative chemotherapy coefficient here
is likely driven by mortality (and by confounding by indication in these
observational data), not by a protective effect on readmission.

### Cumulative baseline mean

`baseline()` returns the estimated cumulative baseline mean with pointwise
95% confidence limits.

```{r baseline}
bl <- baseline(fit_rd)
plot(bl$time, bl$Lambda, type = "s", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Days since surgery", ylab = expression(hat(Lambda)(t)),
     ylim = range(c(bl$lower, bl$upper), na.rm = TRUE))
lines(bl$time, bl$lower, type = "s", lty = 2, col = "grey50")
lines(bl$time, bl$upper, type = "s", lty = 2, col = "grey50")
```

### Prediction

`predict()` evaluates the estimated marginal mean number of readmissions at new
covariate values. Here we compare patients with and without chemotherapy,
for a man with Dukes' stage C and Charlson index 0.

```{r predict}
newdat <- data.frame(chemo    = c("NonTreated", "Treated"),
                     sex      = "Male",
                     dukes    = "C",
                     charlson = "0")
pred <- predict(fit_rd, newdata = newdat, times = seq(0, 1460, by = 7))
head(pred)

plot(pred$time, pred$mu_1, type = "n",
     xlab = "Days since surgery",
     ylab = "Marginal mean number of readmissions",
     ylim = range(pred[, -1]))
polygon(c(pred$time, rev(pred$time)), c(pred$lower_1, rev(pred$upper_1)),
        col = adjustcolor("black", 0.12), border = NA)
polygon(c(pred$time, rev(pred$time)), c(pred$lower_2, rev(pred$upper_2)),
        col = adjustcolor("firebrick", 0.15), border = NA)
lines(pred$time, pred$mu_1, type = "s", lwd = 2)
lines(pred$time, pred$mu_2, type = "s", lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")
legend("topleft", legend = c("No chemotherapy", "Chemotherapy"),
       lty = c(1, 2), col = c("black", "firebrick"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

The shaded areas are pointwise 95% confidence limits for each curve, computed
with the delta method from the sandwich covariance of
$(\hat\beta, \hat\Lambda)$. They describe the uncertainty of each predicted
curve separately; whether the two groups differ is assessed by the
coefficient of `chemoTreated` in the model summary.

---

## Standard errors

| Value | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `"sandwich_adj"` | Sandwich variance estimator with correction for the estimated censoring weights (default) |
| `"sandwich"` | Sandwich variance estimator without the correction |
| `"fisher"` | Inverse Fisher information |
| `"none"` | No standard errors; faster, useful for profiling |

The subject-wise scores and the correction for the estimated inverse
probability of censoring weights are computed with TMB, so standard errors
are fast also for larger data sets.

---

## S3 methods and helpers

| Function | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| `print(fit)` | Compact coefficient table with z-values and p-values |
| `summary(fit)` | Adds the cumulative baseline at tau/4, tau/2, tau |
| `coef(fit)` | Named coefficient vector |
| `vcov(fit)` | Full variance-covariance matrix for (beta, Lambda) |
| `logLik(fit)`, `AIC(fit)`, `BIC(fit)` | Log-likelihood and information criteria |
| `baseline(fit)` | Cumulative baseline mean with pointwise confidence limits |
| `predict(fit, newdata)` | Marginal mean at new covariate values |
| `plot_loglik()` | Profile log-likelihood over the transformation parameter |
| `bladder_prep()`, `readmission_prep()` | Example data sets |
